title: How HEX to RGB Works: Conversion, Alpha, and Picker Limits
description: From HEX digit splitting and the 3-digit shorthand to RGB and HSL rounding, the two alpha scales, and the real limits of sRGB, screens, and pickers.
content:
Converting HEX to RGB is straightforward: split #RRGGBB into three pairs of hexadecimal digits and convert each pair to a decimal value from 0 to 255 using powers of 16. For example, #c9a96e splits into c9, a9, and 6e, which gives rgb(201, 169, 110). The three-digit shorthand has to be expanded to six digits first. What actually goes wrong is alpha, rounding, and differences between screens, not this conversion step.

Split HEX into three pairs, then convert by powers of 16

One hexadecimal digit represents 0–15, and two digits mean the high digit times 16 plus the low digit. c9 is 12 × 16 + 9 = 201, a9 is 10 × 16 + 9 = 169, and 6e is 6 × 16 + 14 = 110. The three pairs map to red, green, and blue in that fixed order, and they cannot be swapped. Write those three steps as a script and you have the most common HEX-to-RGB implementation:

const hex = '#c9a96e';
const value = hex.replace('#', '');
const rgb = [0, 2, 4].map((i) => parseInt(value.slice(i, i + 2), 16));
console.log(rgb); // [201, 169, 110]

The three-digit form is not about “leaving out a few zeros”; each digit is repeated once: #c9a expands to #cc99aa, that is, rgb(204, 153, 170), and #f0a expands to #ff00aa. In the four-digit form #RGBA, the first three digits repeat the same way as #RGB, and only the last digit is alpha: #c9a8 expands to #cc99aa88. That is not the three-digit shorthand with one extra digit appended; the two notations mean different things.

NotationMeaningThis tool
#RGBThree-digit shorthand; each digit repeated onceAccepted
#RRGGBBEight bits each for red, green, and blueAccepted
#RGBAFour-digit form; the last digit is alphaNot accepted
#RRGGBBAAEight-digit form; the last two digits are alphaNot accepted
rgb(r, g, b)Three integers from 0–255Accepted; rgb() optional
rgb(r g b / a)Modern space-separated form, may carry alphaNot accepted
hsl(h, s%, l%)Hue angle and two percentagesAccepted; hsl() optional

The tool is a little more forgiving with HEX than CSS is: the # is optional, leading and trailing spaces are trimmed, and case does not matter.

HSL is another coordinate system for the same color

HSL rewrites an sRGB color as three coordinates: hue (H), saturation (S), and lightness (L). H runs from 0–360, and S and L run from 0–100%. An L of 0 is black, 100% is white, and 50% is “normal”; when S is 0 the color collapses to gray. The same #c9a96e can be written as hsl(39, 46%, 61%). The two point at the same sRGB color; they are not two copies of data in two different color spaces.

Hue is an angle, so a full turn brings you back to the start and 360° is equivalent to 0°. The tool accepts hsl(360, 100%, 50%), treats it as 0° when converting, and still returns #ff0000. It does not accept negative angles, a deg suffix, the modern space-separated syntax, or an alpha argument inside HSL. Saturation and lightness must carry a percent sign, so hsl(120, 100, 50) is rejected.

The HSL conversion itself is reversible; the real loss of precision happens at display time. The interface rounds H, S, and L to integers before writing them into the input fields, and the values you copy out are those rounded strings.

Alpha: 0–1 and 0–255 are two different scales

CSS expresses alpha as a number from 0–1 or as a percentage from 0%–100%, where 0 is fully transparent and 1 is fully opaque; when omitted it defaults to 100%. Eight-digit HEX writes alpha as two hexadecimal digits in the range 00–ff, which is 0–255. Take semi-transparent black: in CSS you write rgb(0 0 0 / 50%), and in eight-digit HEX you write #00000080. The two are not exactly equivalent: 0x80 is 128, 128 ÷ 255 ≈ 0.502, roughly 50.2%, so #00000080 is only the closest 8-bit representation of 0.5.

Converting is just dividing by 255: for #c9a96e80 the alpha is 0x80 = 128 and 128 ÷ 255 ≈ 0.502, about 50.2%. Going the other way, an alpha of 0.5 times 255 gives 127.5, which rounds to 128, written in hexadecimal as 80. W3C serialization rules also work in 8 bits when alpha is stored internally as an 8-bit integer: an internal value of 237 serializes to 0.93, while 236 has no exact two-decimal form, so it outputs 0.92549. This shows that “0–1” and “0–255” are two scales for the same opacity range; conversion always brings rounding with it and cannot be treated as exact equivalence.

This tool only handles opaque colors: HEX accepts three or six digits, and neither RGB nor HSL takes an alpha argument. When you need a translucent color, convert the base color to #RRGGBB first, then record alpha separately and assemble the target format, whether #RRGGBBAA, rgb(r g b / a), or rgba(r, g, b, a). Do not paste eight-digit HEX into the tool; it will not trim the last two digits for you.

Round-tripping the displayed HSL shifts the color

The interface shows rounded HSL. For example, #c9a96e displays as hsl(39, 46%, 61%), while the exact value is hsl(38.9011, 45.7286%, 60.9804%). Note that S and L need their % signs; without them the string is neither valid CSS nor accepted by the tool. Keeping only integers obviously loses information, but how much can be measured by exhaustive enumeration.

Run “RGB → HSL → round → RGB” on all 16,777,216 integer sRGB colors and 15,001,662 of them change in at least one channel, which is 89.42%; the largest single-channel deviation is 5. A deviation of 1 level is the most common, at 9,123,252 colors; only 108 colors deviate by 5. An extreme case is #000001: its HSL lightness is just 0.1961%, which rounds to 0% and turns the color into pure black #000000. Another example is #02e4e6, whose exact HSL is hsl(180.5263, 98.2759%, 45.4902%) (again with the % signs); rounded to hsl(181, 98%, 45%) it comes back as rgb(2, 223, 227), with the green channel off by 5 and blue by 3.

As a control, the same functions with no rounding, going through floating-point HSL, change none of the 16,777,216 colors. The conversion formula is fine; the error comes from display precision. Treat HEX or RGB as the source of truth and HSL as an approximate expression for editing, and you avoid this trap; when you really need exact HSL, keep the decimals instead of relying on what the interface writes back.

Typing, copying, and derived colors in this tool

Open Color converter and picker. The page has a color picker and three text inputs for HEX, RGB, and HSL. The picker updates live on the input event; the three text fields do not sync on every keystroke, but convert and update the other two fields and the preview only after they lose focus (change) or you press Enter. The three copy buttons give you #rrggbb, rgb(r, g, b), and hsl(h, s%, l%) respectively; HEX is always lowercase six digits, RGB is always integers, and HSL is always integers plus percent signs.

  • The HEX input accepts #RGB and #RRGGBB; the # is optional and either case works.
  • RGB takes exactly three comma-separated integers, each between 0–255; percentages, decimals, and alpha are all rejected.
  • HSL hue may be a decimal but must fall within 0–360; saturation and lightness must be written as 0%–100% and cannot drop the percent sign.
  • When the format does not match, the field is marked invalid with a hint and the preview keeps the last valid color; there is no partial parsing.

Below the preview there are three derived-color buttons: complementary, lightness −20%, and lightness +20%. The complementary color adds 180° to the hue and takes it modulo 360; the lightness buttons subtract or add 20 from L and clamp to 0–100. A color with L≤20 therefore clamps to 0 and turns black on “lightness −20%”, and one with L≥80 reaches 100% and turns white on “lightness +20%”; in between, lightness only shifts by 20 points. Gray has no hue, so its complementary color is the same gray. These derivations are only good for quick approximations; a production palette should still be written with explicit values.

To put color values into a stylesheet, you can check declarations and indentation with the CSS formatter; to verify how a channel's decimal and hexadecimal forms correspond, use the base converter to recompute equations such as 0xc9 = 201.

Color difference is not numeric difference

Two colors that differ by 30 numerically do not necessarily look 30 apart. W3C gives a direct example in CSS Color 4: hsl(220 100% 50%) and hsl(250 100% 50%) differ by 30° of hue and look fairly similar, while hsl(50 100% 50%) and hsl(80 100% 50%) also differ by 30° yet look very different. HSL hue angles are not perceptually uniform, so a difference in degrees is not a difference in appearance.

RGB channels behave the same way: adding 10 to each channel does not produce the same lightness change in dark and bright areas, because sRGB channel values are gamma-encoded and are not linear light. HSL's L is only the lightness axis of that cylindrical coordinate system; it is not relative luminance weighted by linear light, and it is not accessibility contrast either. The preview here chooses between black and white text based on relative luminance, but that is the only choice it makes and it does not output a contrast ratio (this tool does not compute contrast; use another tool when you need that). Readability still has to be checked for each foreground and background pair.

The picker, screens, and color gamut

The picker is the browser's <input type="color">; its interface is decided by the browser and operating system and may be a system color panel or a custom window. Its value is normalized to seven lowercase hexadecimal digits, #rrggbb; this page does not enable the alpha attribute, so whatever you pick is always opaque.

Screen state affects “the color you see” and screen sampling, not the conversion itself: an uncalibrated display, different brightness, or night mode and eye-care modes all make the same swatch look different, and a screen eyedropper may sample a shifted value. Once you have the exact HEX number, though, converting between HEX, RGB, and HSL is unaffected by those settings. MDN also warns that however precisely a color is defined, its actual appearance can still vary because devices are uncalibrated or browsers do not support the color profile of the output device. Colors in a web page with no declared color profile are treated as sRGB, while wide-gamut spaces such as Display P3 cover more than sRGB; squeeze a wide-gamut color into sRGB numbers and the out-of-range part can only be clipped or mapped. This tool converts sRGB numbers, does not do gamut mapping, and does not handle CMYK for print.

So picking a color needs at least two confirmations: sample it once against the actual background on the target device, then check the HEX value again on another screen or device.

Boundaries and limits

These limits come from the tool's actual implementation and from the CSS specifications; do not guess when you hit one:

  • Opaque colors only: HEX is limited to three and six digits, and neither RGB nor HSL accepts alpha; four- and eight-digit HEX are judged invalid and are not silently truncated.
  • Alpha has two scales: CSS uses 0–1 or percentages, eight-digit HEX uses 0–255; conversion divides by 255, so state which scale you mean before writing a value into a design file or an API.
  • Shorthand rules differ: in #RGB each digit is repeated once; the fourth digit of #RGBA is alpha. Treating the four-digit form as “three digits plus zero” gives a completely different color.
  • Display precision is limited: the interface HSL is rounded before it goes back into the input, and exhaustive testing shows 89.42% of colors shift in at least one channel, by up to 5; use HEX or RGB when you need exact values.
  • sRGB numbers only: wide gamut, HDR, and CMYK are out of scope; equal numbers do not mean the colors look the same on different screens or with different color profiles.
  • Screen sampling depends on the environment: an eyedropper value can be affected by display calibration, brightness, and system color settings, and picker interfaces differ between browsers and platforms; a HEX value you already have does not change with the screen.
  • No contrast verdict: the preview text only chooses between black and white and does not compute contrast; HSL's L is not a substitute for relative luminance.
  • Invalid input is not repaired: missing digits, out-of-range values, and wrong separators all raise an error, and the preview stays on the last valid color.

An executable checking order

  1. First confirm the format of the source value: is it three-, six-, or eight-digit HEX, integer RGB, or CSS syntax with percentages?
  2. Convert the base color into three integers from 0–255, then decide whether to express it as HEX, RGB, or HSL.
  3. If transparency is needed, record alpha separately, use one scale consistently (0–1 or 0–255), and state which one in the deliverable.
  4. Copy the result back once: paste it into the input and confirm the preview does not jump; a jump usually means rounded HSL was used in between.
  5. Finally check it on the target background and target device; do not mistake “the conversion is correct” for “the display matches”.

Fix these steps and converting among HEX, RGB, and HSL becomes a single, checkable numeric conversion rather than repeated eyeballing and tweaking.
focus: Split HEX into three 0–255 values first, then decide whether to express them as RGB or HSL.
notice: The conversion runs in your browser and no color value is uploaded; transparency and screen gamut are out of scope, so verify on the target background and device before shipping.

faqs.q: Eight-digit HEX is still a color, so why does the tool reject it?
faqs.a: The eight-digit form is #RRGGBBAA, and the last two digits are alpha. This tool only parses the three- and six-digit RGB part, so it reports the value as invalid. When you need a translucent color, convert the first six digits and handle alpha separately on the 0–255 or 0–1 scale.

faqs.q: Can the L in HSL be used as brightness or contrast?
faqs.a: No. L is the lightness axis inside HSL coordinates; it is neither relative luminance nor accessibility contrast. The preview only chooses between black and white text and does not output a contrast ratio, so readability has to be calculated separately.

faqs.q: Why does the color change when I copy HSL and paste it back into the tool?
faqs.a: The interface displays and copies rounded integer HSL. Exhaustively testing all 16,777,216 colors, 89.42% shift in at least one channel after a rounded-HSL round trip, with a maximum shift of 5; using HEX or RGB as the source of truth avoids the problem.

faqs.q: What is the difference between three-digit and four-digit HEX?
faqs.a: Three-digit #RGB is a red-green-blue shorthand where each digit is repeated once; the last digit of four-digit #RGBA is alpha. The two are not related by “padding with zeros”, and the four-digit form cannot be used directly as a three-digit color.
